public_rationale: The Nature abstract, published August 28, 2024, reports negative dialect-based stereotypes about speakers of African American English and describes overt stereotypes about African Americans as “more positive” [e1]. This supports the claimed contrast in the study’s measures, with “fine” understood as comparatively favorable rather than free of overt bias [e1].
limitations: The abstract does not establish that every tested model was free of overt bias.
The findings do not establish how all LLMs behave in unrestricted conversations or actual consequential decisions.
The cited abstract appeared after Marcus’s March 5 post; e1 identifies it as corroborating the findings originally reported March 1, rather than reporting a new August experiment.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: LLMs tested looked fine on overt racism measures but did very badly on covert racism measures when prompted with African American English.

statement.excerpt: On overt measures, the systems were fine. On covert measures, they were a disaster:

from_speaker: On covert measures, they were a disaster
our_interpretation: The surrounding discussion identifies the systems and measures as those in Hofmann and colleagues’ newly released study.
The ordinary reading is a marked contrast between generally favorable overt associations and strongly negative dialect-based associations. 'Fine' is not interpreted as a guarantee of zero overt bias.
The target is the study reported before the post. Its experimental dates are unspecified, so the target period has no invented lower bound.
criteria.support_condition: The cited study finds generally favorable overt associations with African Americans alongside strongly negative associations with speakers of African American English.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The study finds no substantial covert prejudice, or finds overt associations comparably negative rather than the claimed contrast.
